- **Three-level structure (secondary source):** One summary describes the layers as metadata always in the system prompt (roughly 100 tokens per skill), the body loaded on trigger (under about 5k tokens), and resources or scripts loaded on demand.

The search returned mostly third-party guides rather than Anthropic's official documentation, so treat these as community advice.

**Core structure.** A skill is a folder holding a SKILL.md file. The file uses YAML frontmatter with name and description fields, both required, followed by markdown instructions. Personal skills live in ~/.claude/skills/, and project skills in .claude/skills/ can be committed so a team shares them (Personal skills at ~/.claude/skills/your-skill/ are available across all your projects.).

**Description matters most.** One guide says the description drives triggering and deserves the most writing effort, and that the body matters less by comparison (The description field is the trigger. Spend most of your writing time there, not on the body.). Another recommends specific trigger phrases and a gerund-style name such as "writing-release-notes" (Anthropic recommends gerund form: writing-release-notes, prioritizing-backlog. Vague descriptions don't get auto-invoked.).

**Keep it lean.** Loading works in stages: at startup only the name and description of each skill are loaded, and the full SKILL.md only gets read when relevant. Supporting scripts, templates, and reference docs can sit alongside the file and be referenced from it (bundle supporting files such as scripts, templates, reference docs, and example outputs in the same directory, and reference them from the SKILL.md).

**Avoid redundant skills.** One writing-skills guide advises against making a skill for standard practices, one-off fixes, or project conventions that belong in CLAUDE.md (Don't create for one-off solutions, standard well-documented practices, project-specific conventions (use CLAUDE.md), or mechanically enforceable constraints.).

**Testing.** Suggested checks include running the task without invoking the skill by name to see whether it loads on its own, and testing a baseline without the skill to confirm it adds value (Test by asking Claude to do the task without the slash command, then check whether the skill loaded. If not, the description is too vague.).

content.text:
Two searches turned up mostly community guides plus one Anthropic engineering post. I haven't checked any of this against Anthropic's official authoring docs.

## Best practices for Claude Code skills

**Structure**
- A skill is a folder with a `SKILL.md`. It has YAML frontmatter (`name` and `description`, both required) followed by markdown instructions.
- Personal skills go in `~/.claude/skills/`. Project skills go in `.claude/skills/`, which you can commit so the team shares them.
- Put supporting scripts, templates, reference docs and example outputs in the skill folder, and link to them from `SKILL.md`.

**The description matters most**
- Claude uses the description to decide whether to trigger the skill, so spend most of your writing effort there.
- Say what the skill does and when to use it. Include specific trigger phrases, because vague descriptions don't get auto-invoked.
- Write it in the third person.
- Don't summarize the workflow in the description. One secondary source says the model then follows the description and skips the body. I couldn't confirm that claim.
- Use a descriptive, gerund-style name, such as `writing-release-notes`.

**Progressive disclosure**
- At startup Claude loads only each skill's name and description. It reads the full `SKILL.md` when the skill looks relevant, and reads bundled files only when needed.
- Keep the body lean and move detail into separate reference files.
- One secondary source gives rough sizes of about 100 tokens for metadata and under about 5k tokens for the body. I couldn't confirm those figures.

**When not to write a skill**
- Skip one-off fixes and standard, well-documented practices.
- Put project conventions in `CLAUDE.md` instead.
- Skip anything a linter or hook can enforce mechanically.

**Testing**
- Ask for the task without naming the skill. If it doesn't load, the description is too vague.
- Compare against a baseline run without the skill to confirm it adds value.

Sources:
- [Lessons from building Claude Code: How we use skills](https://claude.com/blog/lessons-from-building-claude-code-how-we-use-skills)
- [Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills (Anthropic Engineering)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agent-skills)
- [How to create a Claude Code skill (and the best practices nobody put in the docs)](https://codemeetai.substack.com/p/how-to-create-a-claude-code-skill)
- [How to Write Skills for Claude Code and Cowork](https://sherlock.xyz/post/how-to-write-skills-for-claude-code-and-cowork)
- [skill writing (skills.sh)](https://www.skills.sh/meriley/claude-code-skills/skill-writing)
- [Production-grade agent skills authoring guide 2026](https://noqta.tn/en/blog/production-grade-agent-skills-authoring-guide-2026)
- [Agent Skills: Progressive Disclosure as a System Design Pattern](https://www.newsletter.swirlai.com/p/agent-skills-progressive-disclosure)
